title: BookMyShow (Ticket Booking)
brief: Design a system like a movie and event ticketing app. People browse shows, pick seats on a map, pay, and get a ticket. The hard part is a small, fixed number of seats that thousands of people want at the same moment, when a popular show goes on sale. No seat may be sold twice, and no seat may stay stuck on a person who walked away.

functional: Show the seat map of a show, with which seats are free.
Let a user pick seats and hold them for a few minutes.
Take payment and confirm the booking.
Release held seats if the user leaves or payment fails.
Send the ticket after a confirmed booking.
Protect the system when a popular show opens.

nonFunctional.name: Correctness
nonFunctional.target: A seat is never sold to two people

nonFunctional.name: Seat map
nonFunctional.target: Loads in under 300 ms at the 99th percentile

nonFunctional.name: Hold
nonFunctional.target: A seat is held for one user for a fixed time, then freed automatically

nonFunctional.name: Durability
nonFunctional.target: A paid booking is never lost

nonFunctional.name: Availability
nonFunctional.target: Browsing stays up even when booking is overloaded

estimate.note: All figures are assumptions for a system like this, not facts about any real service. The point is the ratio: a few hundred seats against hundreds of thousands of people.

outputs.note: A hold store this small fits on one machine.

api.does: Returns the seat map: each seat is free, held or sold. May be a few seconds stale.
Tries to hold all the seats at once. All or none. Returns a holdId and its expiry time.
Starts payment for the held seats. Repeating the call with the same key is safe.
Returns the booking and its ticket once confirmed.
Lets the user give seats back before the timer ends.
Joins the waiting room. Returns a place in line and, later, an entry token.

data.store: Relational database, one row per seat.
data.why: Fixed small set per show. A unique constraint on the sold seat is the final guard against a double sale.
Temporary by nature. Set-if-absent with a TTL is atomic, so two users cannot hold one seat, and expiry frees it with no cleanup job.

data.fields: bookingId, userId, showId, seatIds, status, paymentRef, idempotencyKey
data.why: Money is involved. Needs transactions and a unique idempotency key, so a retry cannot book twice.
Short lived and written at a very high rate during on-sale.

evolution.title: One service, one database
evolution.problem: Start with the simplest thing that works: show the seats, let a user pick one.
evolution.change: The service reads seat rows from the database, and marks a seat sold when the user clicks buy.

evolution.title: Cache the seat map
evolution.problem: Everyone refreshes the map to see what is left. Reads outnumber bookings by a huge factor and the database is the bottleneck.
evolution.change: Serve the seat map from a cache with a short expiry of a second or two. Reads no longer touch the database. A slightly stale map is fine because the real check happens at hold time.
evolution.numbers: thousands of map reads per second become a few database reads

evolution.title: Temporary holds
evolution.problem: Two users see the same seat free and both click. One of them pays for a seat that the other one also paid for.
evolution.change: Picking a seat sets a hold key in a fast store with set-if-absent and an expiry. Only one caller can win. A hold covers all chosen seats or none. If the user leaves, the key expires by itself.
evolution.numbers: 5000 attempts per second on 800 seats: all but a few must fail fast

evolution.title: Payment with a timeout
evolution.problem: Payment takes a minute and can fail or hang. The seat must not stay stuck, and a retried click must not charge twice.
evolution.change: A payment service calls the gateway with an idempotency key. On success it writes the booking in a transaction that checks the seat is still held by this user, with a unique constraint on the sold seat. If the timer ends first, the hold simply expires.

evolution.title: Waiting room at on-sale
evolution.problem: When a hit show opens, hundreds of thousands arrive in one minute. That swamps the booking path, even though only hundreds can win.
evolution.change: A virtual waiting room sits in front. People join a line and are admitted at a fixed rate with a signed entry token. The booking service sees a steady flow instead of a spike.
evolution.numbers: the estimator shows rate, wait and people per seat

evolution.title: Settle unknown payments
evolution.problem: The gateway may time out, or a late success may arrive after the hold expired. The money moved but the booking state is unknown.
evolution.change: A reconciliation worker asks the gateway for the real status of every unfinished payment. Late success re-claims the seat if it is free, otherwise the money is refunded.

evolution.title: Tickets off the hot path
evolution.problem: Sending SMS and email inside the booking transaction makes confirmation slow and tied to outside providers.
evolution.change: After the booking commits, a ticket sender reads the new booking and sends the ticket. A retry never blocks or undoes the booking.

steps.say: The user is admitted from the waiting room with an entry token and opens the show.
The booking service returns the seat map from the cache. Held and sold seats are shown as taken.
The user picks two seats. The service tries to set a hold key for each, only if absent, with a TTL of a few minutes. Both must succeed or both are undone.
The user pays. The payment service sends the charge to the gateway with an idempotency key.
On success, one transaction checks the hold still belongs to this user and writes the booking. A unique constraint on the seat rejects any double sale.
The ticket sender sees the new booking and sends the ticket.
A user holds two seats and then closes the app. Nothing else is done.
After the TTL the hold keys disappear on their own. The seats look free again on the next map refresh.
Another user now holds the same seat successfully.
Meanwhile an earlier payment was still pending, and it finally succeeds at the gateway. The recon worker finds it unfinished.
It asks the payment service to confirm. The seat now belongs to someone else, so the booking is refused.
The payment service refunds the late payment and the user is told. No seat was sold twice.

deepDives.title: Where to enforce one owner per seat
deepDives.question: Two users click the same seat at the same moment. What guarantees only one wins?

options.name: Row lock in the database
options.pros: One system. Strong and simple to reason about.
options.cons: Thousands of people contend for a few rows. Locks queue up and the database melts.

options.name: Hold key in a fast store
options.pros: Set-if-absent with a TTL is atomic and cheap. Expiry needs no cleanup job.
options.cons: A second store to run. If it loses data, holds are lost, so it cannot be the only guard.

options.name: Optimistic update with a unique constraint
options.pros: No locks. The database rejects the second sale for certain.
options.cons: The loser finds out late, after typing card details, which is a bad experience.

deepDives.pick: Hold key in front, unique constraint behind
deepDives.because: The hold store rejects almost every loser in microseconds, cheaply. The unique constraint is the last guard that makes a double sale impossible even if the hold store fails. Use both, because each covers the other's weakness.

deepDives.title: How long to hold, and what releases it
deepDives.question: How long should a seat stay held, and who frees it?

options.name: Short fixed TTL
options.pros: Seats come back fast. Good for hot shows.
options.cons: Slow payers lose the seat mid-payment and feel cheated.

options.name: Long TTL
options.cons: Abandoned seats stay locked. A show can look sold out when it is not.

options.name: TTL that extends once at payment start
options.pros: Fair to people who are actually paying. Idle people still time out.
options.cons: More states to test. Payment must be cancelled if the hold is lost.

deepDives.pick: A few minutes, extended once when payment starts
deepDives.because: Users who are paying deserve a small grace. Idle users are what you want to evict. Expiry by TTL means the system heals even if a server crashes mid-flow.

deepDives.title: Waiting room design
deepDives.question: How do we keep a spike from reaching the booking path?

options.name: Rate limit and return errors
options.cons: Fair for nobody: users hammer retry, the system stays hot, and the first people to retry win.

options.name: Virtual queue with signed tokens
options.pros: Fair by arrival order. Steady load. Users see their place.
options.cons: Needs its own scalable front end, and a way to stop people jumping the line.

options.name: Random lottery at open
options.pros: Removes the race to be first, and bots lose their edge.
options.cons: People dislike luck. Needs a pre-registration step.

deepDives.pick: Virtual queue with signed, short-lived entry tokens
deepDives.because: It turns a spike into a flow the booking path can handle. The token proves a turn was granted and expires, so a shared link is useless. Serve the queue page from static and edge capacity so it survives.

failures.impact: Holds vanish and two users may both think they have a seat.
failures.fix: The unique constraint on the sold seat stops a double sale. Rebuild holds from in-flight bookings. Run it replicated, and fail open to the database guard.

failures.what: Payment succeeds but the app crashes before booking
failures.impact: The user is charged and sees nothing.
failures.fix: Persist the payment intent first, with its idempotency key. The recon worker finishes every intent that has no booking, or refunds it.

failures.what: Double click or client retry on pay
failures.impact: A second charge for the same seats.
failures.fix: The idempotency key makes the second call return the first result. The booking row has a unique key on it.

failures.what: Hold expires during a slow payment
failures.impact: The seat goes to another user while the first user's money is in flight.
failures.fix: Extend the hold when payment starts. If the seat is lost anyway, refund automatically and say so plainly.

failures.impact: Real users find every seat gone in seconds.
failures.fix: Challenge on joining the queue, limit seats per account and per card, and tie the entry token to one user.

scaling.limit: One show is one hot spot, however many servers there are
scaling.lever: Everything for a show is keyed by showId, so route it to one partition. Scale by running many shows in parallel, and keep the hot path on the hold store.

scaling.limit: The waiting room must absorb the whole crowd
scaling.lever: Make it a separate, mostly static service on edge capacity. It only needs a counter and tokens. The booking path never sees the crowd.

scaling.limit: Reads on the seat map grow with the crowd
scaling.lever: Cache at the edge for a second or two. Send only a diff of changed seats over a push channel for the busiest shows.

recap.key: Inventory is tiny and demand is huge, so reject losers early with an atomic expiring hold, protect the front with a waiting room, and let the database make a double sale impossible.
recap.numbers: 800 seats against 500K people. 5000 hold attempts per second means about 6 per seat per second. At 500 admitted per second, the last person waits about 17 minutes.
moves: Cache the seat map and accept slight staleness
Hold seats with an atomic key and a TTL
Confirm with an idempotency key and a unique constraint
Admit people through a waiting room, and reconcile unknown payments
